youtube.baslik: Case: Struggling at School with a Normal Audiogram | Lesson 291 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In a fictional case we evaluate a nine-year-old who struggles at school despite a normal audiogram: peripheral hearing, questionnaires and screening, dichotic, pattern, gap detection and low-redundancy speech tests, the AAA 2010 criterion, referral for comorbid conditions, and classroom accommodations.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: American Academy of Audiology, Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis, Treatment and Management of Children and Adults with Central Auditory Processing Disorder (2010); ASHA, (Central) Auditory Processing Disorders, Technical Report (2005); Musiek and Chermak, Handbook of Central Auditory Processing Disorder; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we evaluate, step by step, a nine-year-old who struggles at school but has a normal audiogram.
We will cover auditory processing screening and the test battery, referral for attention and language assessment, and classroom advice.

maddeler.metin: At home, in quiet: few problems

cumleler: Our case is entirely fictional: a nine-year-old in primary school is brought in at the teacher's suggestion.
The teacher says the child seems not to listen in class and leaves instructions half done.
In the crowded classroom and after recess, the child often asks what was said, and also struggles on the phone.
At home, in quiet and face to face, the family sees no clear problem.
The child had frequent middle ear fluid when younger, and speech also started a little later than in peers.
No attention or language evaluation has been done before.
According to the teacher, the child reads aloud slowly and confuses similar sounds.
The child can follow one-step instructions but gets lost in multistep ones.
The child is easily distracted, and the difficulty grows toward the end of a long lesson.
The hardest setting in class is group work, when several groups talk at the same time.
These complaints may fit an auditory processing difficulty, but they look the same in attention, language and learning difficulties.
Peripheral hearing is always assessed before central tests; air conduction thresholds are five to fifteen decibels HL in both ears.
Bone conduction thresholds are also normal and overlap with air conduction.
The speech recognition threshold is five decibels HL in both ears, in agreement with the pure-tone average.
The word recognition score in quiet is one hundred percent in both ears.
A normal audiogram does not diagnose auditory processing disorder, or APD; it only shows a peripheral loss does not explain the complaints.
Tympanograms are type A in both ears; middle ear function is normal.
Ipsilateral and contralateral acoustic reflexes are present at expected levels.
Otoacoustic emissions, or OAE, are present in both ears.
Normal reflexes and emissions also make a hidden peripheral or neural problem, such as auditory neuropathy, less likely.
On a sentences-in-noise test, however, the result is borderline for the test's age norms.
With normal peripheral hearing, the teacher and family fill in a questionnaire such as the Children's Auditory Performance Scale, or CHAPS.
The questionnaire and short screening tests suggest difficulty with listening in noise and auditory memory.
A screening result is not a diagnosis; it only shows that a detailed evaluation is needed.
Many guidelines recommend diagnostic tests from about age seven, because results vary at younger ages; our child is nine.
Before starting the battery, what is known about the child's attention, language and cognition is noted.
In the dichotic digits test, two digits are presented to each ear at the same time, and the child repeats all four digits heard.
In the frequency pattern test, the child names three-tone sequences of high and low tones in words.

cumleler.yazi: The Gaps-In-Noise test, or GIN, measures the detection of brief changes in sound over time.
cumleler.ses: The Gaps-In-Noise test, or G I N, measures the detection of brief changes in sound over time.

cumleler: The filtered speech test assesses low-redundancy listening with words whose high-frequency components have been filtered out.
A speech-in-noise test completes the profile.
Tests use recorded stimuli, start after practice items show the task is understood, and are given in the morning when the child is rested.
The graph shows each test result as the number of standard deviations from the norm for the child's age.

cumleler.yazi: Blue bars are results within the norm: the right ear on dichotic digits, GIN, filtered speech and speech in noise.
cumleler.ses: Blue bars are results within the norm: the right ear on dichotic digits, G I N, filtered speech and speech in noise.

cumleler: Red bars are those more than two standard deviations below: the left ear on dichotic digits and both ears on the frequency pattern test.
A right ear advantage on dichotic tests is normal, but the difference here is larger than the age norm expects.
Low scores in both ears on the frequency pattern test are common, because verbal labeling needs both hemispheres to work together.
The speech-in-noise result is borderline and is not considered significant on its own.
The child was motivated throughout testing and attention was well maintained; this observation also goes into the report.
The two thousand ten guideline of the American Academy of Audiology contains a widely cited criterion.
According to it, results must fall below the norm on at least two different tests, in at least one ear.
This difference must be two standard deviations or more below the norm.
In our case, the dichotic digits and frequency pattern tests meet this criterion.
The criterion supports a profile consistent with APD, but diagnosis is made with the team and physician after comorbidities are assessed.
In a dichotic test, verbal information entering the left ear first reaches the right hemisphere.
To reach the left hemisphere, which is dominant for language, it must cross the corpus callosum.
Naming a frequency pattern in words also requires transfer between the two hemispheres.
So a low left ear on dichotic digits plus low scores in both ears on the pattern test raises the question of interhemispheric transfer.
This is a direction for interpretation, not a diagnosis; the profile guides intervention planning.
APD often occurs together with other developmental conditions; this is called comorbidity.

cumleler.yazi: The most frequent co-occurrence is with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD.
cumleler.ses: The most frequent co-occurrence is with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or A D H D.

cumleler: The child is referred to a child and adolescent psychiatrist for attention and to a speech-language pathologist for language.

cumleler.yazi: For the reading difficulty, an educational assessment with the school and, in Türkiye, the Guidance and Research Center (RAM) is discussed.
cumleler.ses: For the reading difficulty, an educational assessment with the school and, in Türkiye, the Guidance and Research Center (R A M) is discussed.

cumleler: The pediatrician is also part of the process for general health and development.
These evaluations are not done to rule out APD, but to see all of the child's needs.

sahneler.metin: Do not count a low score as APD right away. Attention, fatigue and language easily disrupt central tests.
cumleler: A clinical tip: auditory processing tests are very sensitive to attention, motivation and language skills.
A low score from a tired or unwilling child may reflect the child's state at that moment more than an auditory problem.
Give the battery when the child is rested, split it into two sessions if needed, and note behavior during testing.
Low results on language-based tests with normal results on tests with little language load suggest language and attention factors.
The child should sit near the teacher but away from noise sources such as doors and windows.

cumleler.yazi: Classroom noise should be reduced; the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association recommends a classroom SNR of at least plus fifteen dB.
cumleler.ses: Classroom noise should be reduced; the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association recommends a classroom S N R of at least plus fifteen decibels.

cumleler: A remote microphone system, which sends the teacher's voice directly to the child, can be evaluated with a trial period.
Writing key instructions on the board as well, and breaking multistep instructions into parts, is helpful.
The teacher can check understanding by having the child repeat the instruction in their own words.
These classroom accommodations are given to the teacher as a short written list.
The family is told that the child may have difficulty not in hearing, but in processing what is heard in noise and fast speech.
The teacher receives three to five concrete tips in writing that can be applied right away.
The remote microphone trial is evaluated with teacher and parent questionnaires before and after the trial.
Based on the profile, auditory training targeting dichotic listening may also be planned.
A reevaluation is done in about six months, together with the results of the comorbidity assessments.
Example report language: pure-tone thresholds, immittance findings and OAEs are within normal limits in both ears.
Scores over two standard deviations below age norms were found for the left ear on dichotic digits and both ears on frequency patterns.

cumleler.yazi: Attention and cooperation were good throughout testing; GIN and filtered speech were within normal limits.
cumleler.ses: Attention and cooperation were good throughout testing; G I N and filtered speech were within normal limits.

cumleler: Findings show a profile consistent with an auditory processing difficulty; attention, language and educational assessments are recommended.
Classroom recommendations and a remote microphone trial are attached.
In a child struggling at school, peripheral hearing is first fully assessed with pure tones, speech, immittance and OAEs.
The APD battery measures different processes; scores two standard deviations below norm on two tests, in one ear or more, support diagnosis.
Attention, language and learning difficulties often co-occur and are assessed by the relevant specialists; diagnosis is a team decision.
Classroom advice and the remote microphone are passed to the teacher as a short written list.

sahneler.soru: According to AAA 2010, which finding supports APD?
secenekler: Two SD below on two tests
sahneler.aciklama: Two standard deviations below on at least _two tests_, in at least one ear.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: according to the two thousand ten criterion of the American Academy of Audiology, which finding supports an APD diagnosis?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: performance two standard deviations below the norm on at least two tests, in at least one ear.
A single low score is easily explained by attention or fatigue, and a normal audiogram alone does not diagnose anything.
